newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Iraq's Saddam isolated but opposition deeply split.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Saddam isolated but opposition deeply split.

text.p: President Saddam Hussein, who reacted to U.S. missile attacks on Iraq with a blast of typically defiant rhetoric, is increasingly hemmed in after 17 years in power but opposition to his rule remains deeply split.
In 1979, he inherited a powerful and respected state beginning to flex its muscles as a regional power.

Seventeen years later, isolated and cocooned in his palaces, shackled by tough U.N. sanctions, Saddam rules over a country where many children go hungry, professors moonlight as taxi drivers and law and order depends on draconian punishments.

His plans to build powerful weapons including a "Doomsday gun" lie in tatters as U.N. arms inspectors sift evidence of a crash programme to build a nuclear bomb, long-range missiles and chemicals that could wipe out large populations.
Since the Gulf War over Kuwait in 1991, when he threatened "the mother of all battles", Saddam has not set foot outside his country and rarely appears in public.
Critics say he has only himself to blame for his isolation, mainly through disastrous and costly foreign adventures -- invading first Iran in 1980 and then Kuwait in 1990.
But he has now survived more than six years of the U.N. sanctions imposed after the invasion of Kuwait, including a ban on the oil exports which financed his heyday.

In August 1995, it appeared that his hold on power might be weakening when two sons-in-law, men close to the centre of power, defected to Jordan with tales of family conflict, brutal torture and deliberate deception of the U.N. arms inspectors.
But the defections failed to inspire an uprising against Saddam. Six months later the sons-in-law returned home and were killed, Iraq said, by angry relatives.
Saddam and his advisers, apparently responding to the defections, launched a presidential referendum in October 1995 -- an election he won with more than 99 percent of the vote.
Saddam was born on April 28, 1937, in al-Awja village outside the town of Tikrit, 150 km (93 miles) north of Baghdad.
His father died nine months later and he was raised by an uncle. By 1953, at age 16, he was already in trouble with the monarchy's police for his political activities.
He moved to Baghdad at 18, was drawn into student politics, joined an uprising against the pro-British royalist rulers in 1956 and then became a Baath party militant.
In 1959, after the overthrow of the monarchy, he took part in an attempt to kill President Abdel-Karim Kassem.

The plot was uncovered and Saddam fled to Egypt and then Syria. He returned to Baghdad when the Baath party seized power in a military coup in 1963, but nine months later he was on the run again after the Baathists were toppled.
He was caught, jailed, and released in 1966. He helped plot the July 17, 1968, coup that put the Baath party back in power.
As deputy chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council, he swiftly emerged as the power behind ailing President Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr, whom he eventually succeeded in 1979.

In one of his first major ventures abroad, he signed in 1975 the fateful Algerian agreement, under which Iraq ceded sovereignty over part of the Shatt al-Arab waterway in exchange for an end to Iranian support for a Kurdish rebellion.
When Egypt broke with the Arab consensus and signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, Saddam saw a chance to propel his country into leadership of the whole Arab nation.

The Islamic revolution in neighbouring Iran later in the same year was both a threat and an opportunity. The turmoil weakened Iran but Saddam was worried that Shi'ite radicalism might appeal to the Shi'ite majority in his own country.

In September 1980, after weeks of cross-border shelling along the Shatt al-Arab, Saddam tore up the Algiers agreement and launched a blitzkrieg invasion apparently designed to grab the mainly Arab oil-producing province of Khozistan.
He seriously underestimated the strength and resilience of Iranian nationalism and it took him eight years to extract his country from a war that he could not win.

By the time of a ceasefire with Iran in 1988 Iraq was heavily indebted, especially to the rich Gulf states, and Saddam depended wholly on oil revenues to rebuild the country and push ahead with his arms programmes.
The debts and the need to push up oil prices, as well as Saddam's belief that wealthy Kuwait would be an easy prey, led Iraq into the most disastrous adventure of all.
Iraqi tanks rumbled into Kuwait on August 2, 1990.
Hundreds of thousands of U.S. and allied troops flooded into Saudi Arabia in an attempt to persuade Saddam to withdraw.
He banked on splits in the Western alliance, on U.S. fears of high casualties, on upheaval in the Arab world and on hopes his Scud missiles would bring Israel into the fighting.
When it came, the ground war was over in 100 hours. The remnants of the Iraqi army staggered home and rebellions broke out in the Shi'ite south and the Kurdish north.

In the north, U.S. and other Western troops prevented Baghdad from reasserting control over the Kurds. In the south, where U.S. President Bill Clinton has now extended the no-fly zone, they ban Iraqi aircraft and send up their own planes to keep an eye on any Iraqi troop movements.

Saddam married his cousin Sajida Tolfah in 1963 and has two sons and three daughters. His elder son Uday is much in the public eye, as successful businessman, patron of sports organisations and head of a publishing and television empire.
